subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Galactic Cannibalism
description: A quick, practical guide to Galactic Cannibalism.

hook.text: Large galaxies grow by eating smaller ones. The Milky Way is currently devouring several dwarf galaxies.

buildup.text: The Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy is being torn apart right now. Its stars are being absorbed into the Milky Way's halo.

discovery.text: Gaia found tidal streams—long arcs of stolen stars—wrapping around our galaxy like cosmic spaghetti.

twist.text: This isn't rare—it's how galaxies grow. The Milky Way has consumed at least a dozen dwarfs over its lifetime.

climax.text: Andromeda is doing the same. Its halo contains debris from even more consumed galaxies than ours.

punchline.text: Galaxies eat their neighbors to grow. Ours is mid-meal right now.

quiz.question: How do astronomers detect galactic cannibalism?
options: By finding tidal streams—long arcs of stolen stars from consumed galaxies
By observing explosions when galaxies collide
By measuring the temperature changes in consumed galaxies

details.summary: Galactic cannibalism occurs when a large galaxy strips stars and gas from a smaller one through gravitational tidal forces, gradually absorbing it. The Milky Way is currently cannibalizing several dwarf galaxies — their stars are being stretched into tidal streams that can be traced across our sky…
details.whyItMatters: Cannibalism is how large galaxies grow. The Milky Way's history of swallowing smaller galaxies is written in the tidal streams and stellar halos we observe, revealing our galaxy's assembly history over billions of years.
takeaways: Larger galaxies absorb smaller ones through tidal stripping
The Milky Way is currently cannibalizing several dwarf galaxies
Tidal streams record the history of past accretion events

faq.question: Which galaxies is the Milky Way currently consuming?
faq.answer: The Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy is being torn apart, its stars stretched into a stream wrapping around the Milky Way. The Magellanic Clouds are also being tidally disrupted, producing the Magellanic Stream.

faq.question: Is the Milky Way mostly made from smaller galaxies?
faq.answer: Partly. Cosmological models show large galaxies grow through both smooth gas accretion and merger events. The Milky Way's stellar halo — the spherical envelope of old stars — contains debris from 15-20 consumed dwarf galaxies.
